74. The Art of Storytelling

The Art of Storytelling is one of the oldest cultural practices of humanity, being fundamental to the formation of tribes, families and communities. Before written language, early societies relied on oral narratives to interpret their world, preserve history and transmit values. Communities gathered around fires or in communal circles, weaving stories into rituals, dance, religion and social identity. These shared narratives bound individuals to one another and offered belonging, continuity and meaning. Storytelling served as the framework through which communities understood themselves and taught 'life' to the next generation.

The storytelling tradition continued around the family dinner table, where experiences were exchanged, lessons were absorbed, problems were shared and feelings expressed. These conversations nurtured communication skills, emotional intelligence, self-esteem and moral understanding. Through family stories, children developed a sense of self-worth and a feeling of belonging. Storytelling helped them interpret their experiences, navigate challenges and internalise cultural values and traditions. In Asian cultures, it is considered an honour to listen to the stories of the elders.

However, the rise of modern media disrupted these intimate rituals. Television shifted attention from eye-to-eye contact to a shared screen and the advent of TV dinners further normalised eating without meaningful conversation. Social media individualised entertainment, drawing family members into separate worlds. Some surveys indicate that as many as 72% of Americans use social media during a meal. What had once been an active, communal storytelling environment became a passive and fragmented one. These changes weakened traditions that once connected family and preserved generational knowledge.

The past five years have made the importance of storytelling even more urgent. The pandemic fractured daily life, isolating communities, interrupting rituals and creating traumatic experiences via fear, loss and uncertainty. Many, especially children, endured significant emotional disruption. In this context, storytelling re-emerges as a tool of collective healing. Sharing stories of struggle, resilience and renewal helps individuals transform trauma into meaning and recognise their experiences as part of a broader human journey. The hero's journey. Storytelling becomes a form of psychological restoration, turning chaos into coherence.

Recent years have exposed society to an overwhelming flood of information, deeply disturbing revelations and conflicting narratives experienced under silent psychological warfare. It is therefore imperative to develop the ability to understand where stories originated and how they shape perception, identity and belief. Teaching young people how to think critically has become a vital life skill. Intentional storytelling, grounded in truth, empathy and integrity, can counteract confusion and division.

As communities rebuild after years of isolation, storytelling also serves as a bridge back to connection. Whether shared around a table, within cultural rituals, or thoughtfully used in digital media, stories help reweave the social fabric. Storytelling is also essential to spirituality and our connection to the divine. It offers hope by enabling people to imagine futures worth fighting for and to find solutions that can move us from the collective trauma into true freedom. Likewise, when we hear parts of our own story reflected in others, we are reminded of our shared humanity.

Storytelling remains a timeless and essential human practice, connecting and helping us reclaim community in unstable times. Channels like "Back to Light" are focused on the stories inside each of us. Your story matters. If one single person can find healing and resonance from your experience, would it not be the greatest gift to give them hope and inspiration as we sit around a metaphoric fire? We tell stories to always remember where we were and how far we have travelled to be in this moment.

Researchers believe Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night may show the sky before dawn on July 22, 1889. Long considered an imagined scene sketched in mid-June at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, the painting may instead reflect a real view.

Comparing the sky above Van Gogh’s window with the artwork, researchers found the crescent moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster in matching positions. His letters show he explored night-sky ideas in mid-June, while astronomical analysis suggests he completed the painting more than a month later.

The findings reveal how Van Gogh combined observation with his distinctive swirling brushwork.

[Kim et al. (2026), “The actual sky of Van Gogh’s Starry Night: a multidisciplinary reconstruction,” Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-73025-5]
